title: Reading fluently
keyIdea: Fluent reading sounds like talking. You read the words right, at talking speed, with a voice that fits. Read in scoops, groups of words that go together, not one word at a time. Let the end mark set your voice: calm for a full stop, up for a question mark, strong for an exclamation mark. Pick a book where you can read 9 or 10 words out of 10, and read it again and again. Each time, the stops get fewer and the reading gets smoother.

kid: Fluent reading sounds like talking. A robot reads like this: the… big… dog… ran. You can read in scoops. The big dog… ran to the park. Each scoop is a group of words that go together.
Look at the mark at the end. A full stop says: stop, and be calm. A question mark says: you are asking, so let your voice go up. An exclamation mark says: use a strong voice!
Fast is not the best. Too fast and you run past the stops, and it does not make sense. Too slow and you forget the start. Read at talking speed.
Read the same book again. The first time, you may get stuck and sound out a word. The next time it is quicker. Pick books where you can read 9 or 10 words out of 10.
adult: Fluency means reading the words correctly, at a natural pace, with expression. Experts call the expression part prosody. When reading is fluent, your child has more attention left for meaning. The English national curriculum asks Year 1 pupils to read aloud books that match the phonics they know, and to reread them to build fluency and confidence. In Year 2 they read such books accurately, automatically and without undue hesitation. Common Core RF.K.4 asks for emergent-reader texts read with purpose and understanding. RF.1.4b asks for reading aloud with accuracy, appropriate rate and expression on successive readings.

Key words: accuracy (words read correctly), automaticity (knowing a word at once, with no slow sounding out), rate (how many words are read correctly in a minute), prosody (phrasing, stress and the rise and fall of the voice), phrasing (reading in groups of words that belong together, often called scooping), repeated reading (reading the same text a few times) and a decodable book (one that uses only the phonics your child has been taught). This topic asks for reading with at least 90% accuracy, about 9 words in 10. Many teachers aim higher, about 19 words in 20, for reading alone. Below 9 in 10, read the book together. The DfE reading framework adds that a decodable book should match the sounds already taught, so every word can be sounded out.

Common mistakes: treating speed as the goal, so children race past full stops and lose the meaning; robot reading, one word at a time; a flat voice that ignores question and exclamation marks; books that are too hard, so every line stops for sounding out; reading a book once and moving on; and guessing words from the picture. Be careful not to time children with a stopwatch at this age. Praise smooth rereading with a voice that fits.

In the lab your child taps where the first scoop of a line ends. They drag a calm, asking or excited voice onto lines that end in a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. They read one page three times and see the stops fall from 3 to 1 to none. They sort four books by how many words in 10 they can read. Last, they drag a speed dial to hear why snail and rocket reading both lose the meaning. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Pick a short book your child knows well. Read one page to them like a storyteller, then let them read the same page back to you. Read it again tomorrow. Point out one thing that got better, like a smooth scoop or a question that went up.

visual.caption: Fluent or not yet? Drag each way of reading, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Reads one… word… at… a… time
Voice goes up at a question mark
Reads the book again to get smoother

lab.caption: Flagship lab: scoop words into phrases, set the voice from the end mark, reread a page, pick a just right book and find talking speed.

practice.prompt: Which way of reading sounds most like talking?
choices: My cat… sat on the mat.
My… cat… sat… on… the… mat.
practice.hint: Talking puts words that go together into one group, a scoop.
practice.explain: My cat… sat on the mat reads in two scoops, like talking. One word at a time sounds like a robot, and running it all together is too fast to follow.

practice.prompt: A page has 10 words. You get stuck on {n} of them. How many words can you read?
practice.hint: Take the words you got stuck on away from 10.
practice.explain: 10 take away {n} is {=10-n}. If that is 9 or 10, the book is just right for reading by yourself.

practice.prompt: A line ends with a question mark: Where is my hat? How should your voice go?
choices: Up at the end, like asking
Flat, the same as every line
practice.hint: Look at the mark at the end of the line. What does it tell you?
practice.explain: A question mark means you are asking, so your voice goes up. A strong voice is for an exclamation mark, and a flat voice hides the question.

practice.prompt: Mia reads a page and gets stuck {n} times. Each time she reads it again, she gets stuck 1 time fewer. How many times does she get stuck on her next read?
practice.hint: Take 1 away from the number of times she got stuck.
practice.explain: {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}. Each reread makes the words easier, so the stops go down.

pool.prompt: Leo reads very, very fast. He runs past every full stop. What goes wrong?
choices: His voice goes up too much
pool.hint: Think about what the full stops are for.
pool.explain: Racing past the full stops runs the ideas together, so it stops making sense. Fluent reading is talking speed, not a race.

pool.prompt: Which book is just right to read by yourself?
pool.hint: Just right means only a few words need sounding out.
pool.explain: 9 of 10 words is just right. With 6 or 4 of 10 there are too many stops, so read those books with a grown-up.

pool.prompt: We won the race! How do you read this line?
pool.hint: Look at the mark at the end of the line.
pool.explain: An exclamation mark asks for a strong voice that shows the feeling. A question would end with a question mark.

pool.prompt: What is the best way to get smoother at reading a book?
choices: Look at the pictures and guess
pool.hint: Think about what happens to the stops each time you read the same page.
pool.explain: Rereading the same book makes the words quicker each time, so the reading gets smoother. Guessing from pictures skips the real words.

pool.prompt: Where does the first scoop end in: The little bird sang in the tree.
pool.hint: Ask: who? Then ask: what did it do?
pool.explain: Who? The little bird. What did it do? Sang in the tree. So the first scoop ends after bird.

pool.prompt: Zoe reads: The… dog… is… wet. What can she try?
choices: Read it in scoops: The dog… is wet.
Read it faster with no stops
pool.hint: One word at a time sounds like a robot. Group the words.
pool.explain: Reading in scoops, The dog… is wet, sounds like talking. Going faster or louder does not group the words.

pool.prompt: A line has {n} scoops. Each scoop has 3 words. How many words are in the line?
pool.explain: {n} scoops of 3 words make {=3*n} words. You read each scoop in one go.

pool.prompt: Sam reads a page of 10 words and can read {n} of them. How many does he get stuck on?
pool.hint: Take the words he can read away from 10.
pool.explain: 10 take away {n} is {=10-n}. If he gets stuck on more than 1 word in 10, read the book together.

pool.prompt: Is the cat asleep? and The cat is asleep. have the same words. How do you read them?
choices: The same, because the words match
pool.hint: Look at the two end marks.
pool.explain: The end mark changes the voice. The question goes up, and the full stop line is calm.
